source.title: Improving Generalization and Convergence by Enhancing Implicit Regularization
source.authors: Mingze Wang; Jinbo Wang; Hao-Tian He; Zi-Lin Wang; Guan-Hua Huang; Fei-Yu Xiong; Zhi-Yu Li; E. Weinan; Lei Wu

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present. Some equations and table layout are flattened, but the main results tables are recoverable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether an intervention designed to strengthen implicit sharpness regularization changes generalization and convergence, using IRE rather than the interventions or measurements named in V1–V8. It does not test any listed version as specified.
record.gate_note: The experiments compare IRE variants with base optimizers and report test accuracy or validation loss, and some experiments report sharpness. None tests random-label memorization, width past interpolation, CNN versus fully connected architecture, optimizer comparisons to SGD under the V4 tuning conditions, batch-size effects, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Those results are recorded as findings outside the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses the premise that flatter solutions generalize better to motivate IRE and evaluates its own optimizer modification. It tests none of V1–V8. In particular, its Fisher-trace sharpness measurements and accuracy comparisons do not measure V7's magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, train–test error gaps, or ranking against alternative measures.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors report improved image-classification generalization, accelerated Llama pre-training convergence, and enhanced sharpness reduction. They leave the acceleration mechanism, larger-scale validation, and downstream language-model performance for future work.
record.recipe_differences: IRE modifies base optimizer updates by increasing updates in estimated flat directions. Experiments activate IRE partway through training; vision experiments also use stated data augmentation and label smoothing. This differs from the listed original interventions and measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: IRE settings κ and γ are varied; the paper reports accuracy results across different model and dataset settings. The CIFAR and ImageNet experiments use different base optimizers and training recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: IRE improves reported image-classification accuracy over the corresponding base optimizer in Tables 1–4; the corrected R19 comparison is 78.7% to 79.1%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding IRE can improve held-out image-classification accuracy under the tested training recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: For WRN-16-8 on CIFAR-10, Figure 2 reports lower Fisher-trace sharpness alongside lower training loss and higher test accuracy as IRE strength increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under this SAM-IRE intervention, lower unscaled sharpness trace accompanies improved training loss and test accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Llama-60M with AdmIRE reaches reported loss 2.47 at 50k steps versus AdamW at 100k, with sharpness traces 88.86 versus 120.41.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: AdmIRE can reach matched pre-training loss in fewer updates and produce lower unscaled sharpness trace.

record.problems: The reported main vision tables do not state uncertainty; a separate fixed-hyperparameter table reports averages over 3 random seeds, but the main tables do not. The IRE sharpness measurement uses a Fisher-based approximation to the Hessian trace. The paper says the language-model acceleration mechanism needs further study and downstream performance is left for future work.
record.rows_left_out: Table 4 has a flattened layout; the available text does not securely support mapping all displayed accuracy values to optimizer and γ conditions, so uncertain assignments are not recorded as separate rows. Figure-only curves and the Table 5 per-step wall-clock comparison are omitted because they do not measure a listed claim version or an additional generalization outcome.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization capacity and natural- versus random-label held-out accuracy under the same recipe.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning, and the stated remedies.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty.
Dropout effects, small-data and excessive-dropout regimes, and joint removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance versus train–test error gaps, including comparison with norm- and margin-based rankings.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus equal-sized random removals.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels apply. Figure 2 and Table 8 provide additional results outside the listed versions. The claimed Table 4 ambiguity is resolved by the supplied text and Appendix C.1.2.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy for natural versus random labels.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD under the stated tuning conditions, including the specified reversals and remedies.
Large versus small batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout comparisons, training-set-size conditions, and removal of dropout with weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbation tolerance and its ranking of train–test gaps against other measures.
Removing examples identified as memorized and comparing against random-example removal.
